scanner_doubts: multivariate_normal.md:902 - qe-math-010 (proposed) is measured at 31 and does not include line 902, `Var\left(\theta \mid y_1, \dots, y_k\right) = c^2_{k+1} + \dots`. In `check_math_010` the Roman-spelling branch (`other`, tools/qestyle_rules.py:670-674) requires the operator to carry a backslash (`\Var`) or a wrapper (`\text{Var}`, `\mathrm{Var}`, `\operatorname{Var}`, `{\rm Var}`), and the bare-letter branch (`bare_E`) is written for the single letter `E` only. A variance, covariance or probability operator spelled out as plain letters with no backslash and no wrapper - `Var(`, `Cov(`, `Pr(`, `Prob(` - therefore matches nothing. This is worse than a style miss: with no `\operatorname`, `Var` typesets as the italic product $V\cdot a\cdot r$. Adding a bare-Roman branch, `(?<![\\A-Za-z0-9_{])(?:Var|Cov|Pr|Prob|Cor)\s*(?:\\left)?\s*[(\[]`, catches it; `likelihood_ratio_process.md` in the same series has the same pattern.

multivariate_normal.md:512-513 - qe-writing-004 is measured at 1 (line 2145, 'Components'), but 512-513 reads "A Law of Large / Numbers explains why sample analogues approximate population objects", and both `law` and `numbers` are in `COMMON_NOUNS`. Neither is counted, for two structural reasons in `check_writing_004` (tools/qestyle_rules.py:280-295): the lookbehind `(?<=[a-z,])` requires a lowercase letter or comma immediately before the whitespace, so a capitalised common noun preceded by another capitalised word - here the sentence-opening "A" - is invisible; and the regex runs per source line, so "Numbers" at the start of 513 has no preceding text to match against. Because these lectures hard-wrap prose at ~70 characters, the second gap will silently drop a share of every multi-word capitalised phrase in the corpus. Widening the lookbehind to `(?<=[a-z,A-Z])` and joining a paragraph block before matching would close both.

multivariate_normal.md:782,783,790 - qe-math-001 is measured at 0, but these three matplotlib labels put unicode Greek *inside* `$...$` math delimiters: `label='true $θ$'` (782), `label=r'$\hat{μ}_{θ}$'` (783) and `plt.ylabel(r'$\hat{θ}$')` (790), the middle one mixing unicode μ and θ with the LaTeX `\hat`. The rule's text is unambiguous - "Never use unicode characters inside math environments" - and these strings really are rendered as math by matplotlib's mathtext. The lexer classifies code-cell content as code, which is right for `qe-code-002`'s sake, so this may be a deliberate scope decision rather than a defect; I flag it because it is the one place in the corpus where a math environment lives inside a code cell, and the same three lines are why the file scores 10/10 on Code and clean on Math-001 while shipping `$\hat{μ}_{θ}$`.
